small_guidance:
- The GEMM is the dominant cost (128×16384×16384 ≈ 68 GFLOPs); add larger tile configs to the autotune list (e.g. `BLOCK_M=64/BLOCK_N=256/BLOCK_K=64 num_warps=8 num_stages=4`, `BLOCK_M=32/BLOCK_N=256/BLOCK_K=64`) — M=128 means BLOCK_M>128 is wasted, so favor small M / large N tiles. Also try `num_stages=5` for the K=16384 loop.
- Add a GROUP_M block-swizzle (group size 8) for L2 reuse across N tiles, and drop the `k_remaining` masking in the K loop since K=16384 is divisible by all BLOCK_K choices — unconditional `tl.load` lets the compiler pipeline better.
- For the softmax, BLOCK_N=4096 forces 4 iterations per pass over a 16384-wide row; try BLOCK_N=8192 with num_warps=8 or even BLOCK_N=16384 (single-pass persistent, row fits in regs) to halve the global-memory traffic from 3× read to 2× read.
large_guidance:
- Fuse softmax into the GEMM epilogue using a split-N two-pass strategy: pass 1 has each `(pid_m)` program stream the full K-loop across all N tiles to compute per-row max and sum (writing the GEMM output to a scratch buffer or recomputing); pass 2 normalizes. Better: since M=128 is tiny, use a persistent per-row kernel — one program per row, iterate N tiles, do GEMM-of-row × full-weight with `tl.dot` over (1×BLOCK_K)·(BLOCK_K×BLOCK_N), maintain running max/sum online, then a second pass over N to write normalized outputs. This eliminates the full 128×16384 intermediate write+read.
- Alternatively, keep the GEMM separate but write its output in tiles directly consumed by a fused softmax that runs as the epilogue of the last K-block — requires storing partial GEMM tile to shared and immediately reducing, but with M=128 the whole output row (16384 fp32 = 64KB) doesn't fit in SMEM, so the persistent-row approach above is preferable.
- Consider using tensor cores via tf32 (`allow_tf32=True` / `tl.dot(..., input_precision='tf32')`) — for this dropout+softmax pipeline the loose 5e-2 tolerance easily accommodates tf32 and it ~2× the GEMM throughput on Ampere.
